filelock@4.0.10: On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.  Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.  ## Scope and preconditions  - Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover. - Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete. - Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails. - Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time. - What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits. - Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes. - Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L84-L122) renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. [`_poll_until_acquired`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1378-L1408) and [`_check_give_up`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1590-L1608) test the deadline, `blocking` and `cancel_check` only between attempts.  ## Introduced  [e35c3af](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/e35c3af) "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" ([#476](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/476), 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.  ## Mechanism  Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.  ## Reproduction  The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. filelock@4.0.10: `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4). Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The lock user's `os.open` raises an inotify `IN_OPEN` event. The other user unlinks `cache.lock.db` and links `cache.lock.db.keep` back under the same name. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. None of filelock's checks look at that file. `_open_lock_database` and `_raise_if_wal` inspect descriptor 3. `_raise_if_database_replaced` compares an `lstat` of the lock path with the descriptor's `(st_dev, st_ino)`, which passes because the other user linked the same inode back, and it runs only after `BEGIN`.  The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. Strace of the lock user's process (SQLite 3.40.1):  ``` openat("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0600) = 3 readlink("/proc/3819/fd/3", "/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", 4096) = 41 readlink("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", "/tmp/victim-notes.txt", 4096) = 21 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 4 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal", O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 5 pread64(5, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 516) = 4096 pwrite64(4, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 0) = 4096 unlink("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal") = -1 EPERM            -> "disk I/O error" ```  The redirect itself needs no journal. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a missing path in the lock user's home, constructing the lock created that file (empty, `0644`, owned by the lock user) and raised nothing. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The pragma converted the lock user's database out of WAL mode, and the redirected acquire held its SQLite lock on that database rather than on the lock database.  **Side-file names beside the database.** Two comments record the belief that SQLite names its side files after the descriptor path ([line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), [line 1095](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1095)). The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. These variants need no redirect.  *A hot `-journal` makes the lock user unlink a file the journal names; no race.* The other user unlinks the lock user's empty `lock.db`, puts a one-page SQLite database (`0666`) in its place, and writes a 46-byte `lock.db-journal`: a path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. The code in [`_do_acquire_inner`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) translates only "database is locked" into `Timeout`. `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` therefore leaves every `acquire_read()` / `acquire_write()` (and the async variants) within milliseconds, whatever `timeout` or `blocking` says, until the file's owner or root removes it.  *Further effects observed at this commit in a non-sticky directory.* A `0755` script owned by the lock user, renamed to the lock path with a one-record journal beside it, ends up holding the other user's bytes (the acquire raises `file is not a database`). A hard link to the lock user's `0600` `~/.profile` at the lock path does the same in a sticky `/tmp` when `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. When the locking process runs as root, SQLite runs `fchown` on a `-wal` or `-shm` it opens to match the owner of the database, so root's `0600` `service.env` renamed to `app.lock.db-wal` belonged to the other user after root's `read_lock()`.  A journal whose super-journal names the database itself makes SQLite open and close a second descriptor on the database, which drops the process's POSIX locks, so `acquire_read` returns with no lock held in `/proc/locks` and a writer in another process acquires (two journals in a row, one per statement; write locks are not affected). A one-byte `lock.db-wal` plus a `lock.db-shm` on which the other user holds two byte locks makes the acquire take 10 s regardless of `timeout` and raise `locking protocol`, or die with `SIGBUS` if the other user truncates the `-shm`.  **The hard-link route in a directory without the sticky bit.** None of the above occurs on the `_link_beside` branch (macOS, Linux without `/proc`). There SQLite's main file is `.filelock-…/lock.db` in the connecting user's `0700` directory. That protection holds only where no other user can rename the `.filelock-*` entry itself, because `0700` protects the contents, not the entry in the parent. `_link_beside` checks the link once and returns a pathname, and every later use is by that name.  With `/proc` hidden in a `0777` directory, the other user staged a directory holding a hard link `lock.db` to a one-page database and a hot `lock.db-journal`. They held `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` on the database so the lock user's first statement waited in the busy handler (SQLite's retry loop for a locked database), renamed the lock user's `.filelock-*` directory aside, renamed the staged directory onto its name and rolled back. SQLite got SHARED, found the journal under the swapped name and unlinked the file it named. The lock user's process reported the lock held and exited 0. A polling variant without the write lock also won (in 40 trials the file was gone after 1 to 26 starts of the lock user's program). Under the sticky bit the rename fails with `EPERM`.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J`, quoted as received. '`, after `b"ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE VICTIM'S ReadWriteLock
\x00..."`, verdict `BUG`. Reacting to inotify redirected the first acquire in 77 of 77 runs. A plain unlink/link busy loop with no inotify also won on the first run. A process holding two `ReadWriteLock` instances on one database keeps an idle descriptor; a swap done a full second before the second acquire redirected it. The `-wal` re-plant landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs. The journal-unlink variant needs no race.  Our verification: the reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #834 head it prints `OK`: all 20 `victim` runs exit 0 with no error and the target stays `1000 0o600 22` bytes with its original content. The independent review also ran the sticky-directory `-wal` variant (a `0600` database owned by `victim` in a `1777` directory, other user plants `<db>-wal`). 4.2.0 raises `OperationalError: disk I/O error`; the PR head takes read and write locks with the file still present.  ## Impact  Another local user who can write the non-sticky directory holding the database makes the lock user's process act on a file other than the lock database, with the lock user's privileges, on Linux. The process writes bytes of the other user's choosing from offset 0 into any non-empty regular file the lock user can write, resized to a whole number of pages, provided the other user can create `<file>-journal` beside it (the lock user's own `0600` files in `/tmp` qualify). Without a journal the process creates an empty file at any path it may create, or converts a WAL-mode SQLite database of its own to rollback mode with no error. A journal beside a swapped-in database makes the process unlink one regular file of the other user's choosing per journal; the acquire succeeds and raises nothing. A process inside `write_lock()` stops excluding the lock user's other processes from `read_lock()`, and the holder can die from a `SIGBUS` that arrives in `release()`.  It is **not** reachable for a database the lock user owns in `/tmp` with `fs.protected_regular` 1 or 2. There only the planted `-wal` denial of service remains: every acquire raises an undocumented `sqlite3.OperationalError` that `Timeout` and `OSError` handlers do not catch. It is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (4.0.9), which refused the symlink at the database path but followed it at `<database> (deleted)`. Windows does not take this path.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. - For a lock in a sticky directory keep `fs.protected_regular` at 1 or 2 and `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (distribution defaults). Treat a sudden `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<db>-wal` beside the database that the file's owner or root has to remove.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. certifi@2026.7.22: Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them.   An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. filelock@4.0.10: On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.  Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.  ## Scope and preconditions  - Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover. - Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete. - Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails. - Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time. - What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits. - Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes. - Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4). Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. A hard link to the lock user's `0600` `~/.profile` at the lock path does the same in a sticky `/tmp` when `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. A journal beside a swapped-in database makes the process unlink one regular file of the other user's choosing per journal; the acquire succeeds and raises nothing. A process inside `write_lock()` stops excluding the lock user's other processes from `read_lock()`, and the holder can die from a `SIGBUS` that arrives in `release()`. There only the planted `-wal` denial of service remains: every acquire raises an undocumented `sqlite3.OperationalError` that `Timeout` and `OSError` handlers do not catch. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. - For a lock in a sticky directory keep `fs.protected_regular` at 1 or 2 and `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (distribution defaults).
